chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Ulwan from 'Amr ibn Khalid from Zayd ibn 'Ali from his fathers from 'Ali (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Verily, the lowest in rank among the inhabitants of Paradise, from among the martyrs, is one who will have twelve thousand wives from the wide-eyed houris, four thousand virgins, and twelve thousand non-virgins. Each of these wives will be served by seventy thousand servants, but the wide-eyed houris will have something more. He will go around their gatherings every week, and when the day or the hour of one of them comes, they will gather around her singing in voices so sweet and nice that no other voices can compare, until nothing remains in Paradise but that it is swayed by their voices. They will say, “Indeed, we are immortal, so we will never die; and we are [soft and] tender, so we will never become [wrinkled and] hard; and we are satisfied, so we will never get angry.”'
ai.seo_question: What is the rank and reward of the lowest martyr in Paradise according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from *Kitab al-Zuhd* highlights the concept of *adna* (lowest rank) in Paradise, illustrating that even the least honored martyr enjoys immense, tangible blessings, including twelve thousand wives and seventy thousand servants each. The description emphasizes the sensory and emotional perfection of the hereafter, where the joy of the inhabitants is so profound it causes the entire realm of Paradise to resonate with their voices. This reflects the Shia scholarly view that Paradise is not merely spiritual but also physical, with distinct hierarchies of reward based on merit.

en.shaykh-tahir-ridha-jaffer: 9.Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUlwān narrated from ʿAmr ibn Khālid, from Zayd ibn ʿAlī, from his fathers, from ʿAlī (a) who said,

“The Messenger of Allah (ṣ) said, ‘Verily the lowest of the inhabitants of Paradise in rank among the martyrs [1] is one who will have twelve thousand wives from the wide eyed houris, four thousand virgins, and twelve thousand non-virgins. Each of these wives will be served by seventy thousand servants, but the wide-eyed houris will have something more. He will go around their gatherings every week, and when the day or the hour of one of them comes, they will gather around her singing in voices so sweet and nice that no other voices can compare, until nothing remains in Paradise but that it is swayed by their voices. They will say, “Indeed, we are immortal, so we will never die; and we are [soft and] tender, so we will never become [wrinkled and] hard; and we are satisfied, so we will never get angry.”’”
